sections.h2: Who sets and collects the tax
sections.html:
Property tax on a Virginia house is a local matter. Your county, city, or town sends the bill, not the state, and each one decides its own rates, due dates, and relief programs.

Two offices split the job. The commissioner of the revenue values your property and corrects mistakes. The treasurer takes payment and chases delinquent accounts. You will find both on your locality's website. Request a payoff figure from the treasurer when a closing approaches.

sections.h2: How a house is valued for tax
sections.html:
Real estate is taxable unless an exemption applies, and each reassessment targets 100 percent of fair market value (Va. Code 58.1-3201). Your bill rests on what the locality thinks the house would sell for, whatever you paid.

The schedule varies. A county reassesses every four years, or every three when its board of supervisors votes that way. A county with 50,000 people or fewer can stretch to five or six years, and Augusta and Bedford counties may too (Va. Code 58.1-3252). A county or city that employs a qualified full-time appraiser can pass an ordinance for annual or two-year assessment, valuing property as of January 1 (section 3253).

County general reassessment4 years, or 3 if supervisors vote58.1-3252

Locality with a qualified full-time appraiserEvery 2 years or yearly, by local ordinance58.1-3253

The calendar is a local decision. A locality may bill once or in two equal installments, and it fixes penalties and interest by ordinance (section 3916). Two neighboring localities may not share a schedule, so read the treasurer's calendar for your own address.

Localities cannot pile on charges without limit. Interest can start the next day, at no more than 10 percent a year, with a higher cap from the second year of delinquency onward. A late penalty may reach 10 percent of the overdue amount or $10, whichever is more, but not beyond the tax itself. Fees for collection or attorneys can be added if contracted for, at up to 20 percent of the delinquent tax.

The statute also gives some breathing room:

  • For good cause, a locality may extend payment by as much as 90 days.
  • A service member deployed outside the country is automatically extended on the tax for a primary residence until 90 days after deployment ends.
  • When a local official caused the late assessment, there is no penalty if the bill is paid within two weeks of notice.

Start with the assessor, move on to the local board of equalization, and finish at the circuit court if needed. The board assumes the assessor's number is right and can lower or raise it. You win by showing, with the greater weight of the evidence, that the house is valued above fair market value, or that the assessment is uneven and ignored accepted appraisal practice (section 3379).

Comparable sales through the December 31 before the effective date can be used as evidence, if they reach the locality by its deadline. Owners of a home with under four residential units are entitled to written notice from the assessor, and to the assessment records within 15 days of a written request.

Two other routes remain open:

  • The commissioner of the revenue can correct an error if you apply within three years after the tax year ends or one year after assessment, whichever is later. For real estate this means the commissioner's own mistakes or factual errors in a general reassessment (section 3980).
  • The circuit court takes applications within three years after the last day of the tax year, or one year after assessment or the end of an earlier appeal, whichever is later. It starts from the same presumption of correctness (section 3984).

Appeals work best when you bring paper. Gather your last assessment notice, a few recent sales of similar houses near yours, photos of defects that lower value, and any repair estimates. Put them in order before the hearing, and write down the exact figure you think is fair so the board has something specific to decide on.

While an administrative appeal is pending, the bill does not go delinquent, provided you filed within 90 days of the assessment. The pause extends 30 days past the final decision.

sections.h2: Exemptions and deferrals for older owners
sections.html:
Relief of this kind appears only where a locality has voted for it. Under Va. Code 58.1-3210, a county, city, or town may pass an ordinance that exempts or defers tax for owners age 65 and up, or permanently and totally disabled if the ordinance includes that group, as long as the home is their only dwelling.

An ordinance may limit the break to growth in the tax since the owner turned 65 or became disabled. Homes held through a life estate, a revocable trust the owner controls, or certain irrevocable trusts may qualify. A leasehold does not. Income and net worth limits are local, so ask your local assessing office what applies.

Closing settles the bill. The tax lien sits above all others until the locality is paid, and a purchaser, a foreclosure trustee included, must send proceeds to the taxes and levies on that property (Va. Code 58.1-3340). Penalty and interest are treated as tax here, and current-year rents fall under the lien as well.

The sales contract prorates the seller's share. One timing quirk: a sale after January 1, once bills are out, lets the treasurer withdraw the old owner's bill and send a new one to the buyer, penalty free if paid within two weeks.

A locality can go to court to sell a house over unpaid tax. The usual trigger is taxes still unpaid on December 31 following the second anniversary of the due date. Properties that are condemned, a nuisance, derelict, or designated blighted qualify after one year. A property assessed at $100,000 or less can be sold on a court finding after the first anniversary (Va. Code 58.1-3965).

Before suing, the collecting officer has to send notice to the address on file and to the property at least 30 days in advance, and the list goes into a local newspaper. Paying the full balance before the sale redeems the property, but a partial payment will not end the suit. An installment agreement of up to 72 months can put the sale on hold, so long as current taxes are also kept up.

If the property sells for more than is owed, the former owner and heirs are entitled to the surplus left after taxes, penalties, interest, fees, costs, and liens. Claims must come within two years of confirmation, or the money goes to the locality (Va. Code 58.1-3967).

What you owe at closing counts for more than the offer price. Get a fresh tax statement from the treasurer before accepting anything, and have the title company list each lien. Budget for the state recordation tax of 25 cents per $100 and the grantor tax of 50 cents per $500, which falls on the seller unless the contract moves it (Va. Code 58.1-802).

A sensible routine before you sign anything: pull your latest bill, note whether the first half or both halves are paid, and write down the name and phone number of the treasurer's clerk who gave you the figure. Bring the bill to your first conversation with a buyer. When the numbers on paper match what the title company finds, closing day moves faster and fewer surprises come out of your proceeds.

Tell the title company early if you have an open assessment appeal, a local deferral, or an installment plan with the treasurer. Any of them can change the payoff, and a cash buyer can plan around them when they are disclosed up front.

faqs.q: Who handles questions about my bill?
faqs.a: The treasurer collects it, and the commissioner of the revenue or an equivalent office sets the value. Both are local, not state, offices.

faqs.q: How often does my house get reassessed?
faqs.a: Counties must do it every four years, or every three if supervisors vote for it. Small counties may use five or six years, and a locality with a qualified appraiser can assess every year or every other year.

faqs.q: What is the maximum late charge?
faqs.a: The penalty may reach 10 percent of the overdue tax or $10, whichever is greater, but never more than the tax. Interest is limited to 10 percent a year, higher after the first year of delinquency.

faqs.q: Can I list my house during a tax appeal?
faqs.a: Yes. The tax stays a lien, so closing pays it from proceeds. Tell the title company about the appeal so the payoff comes out right.

faqs.q: When can a locality sell a house for unpaid tax?
faqs.a: Usually after delinquency on December 31 past the second anniversary of the due date. One year is enough for condemned, nuisance, derelict, or blighted property, and for property assessed at $100,000 or less with a court finding.
